questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a correlation establishes and what it leaves undetermined
questions.stem: A transit board sees that months with more bus shelters also have higher ridership and concludes that shelters cause ridership. What does the correlation actually establish?

options.text: Shelter count and ridership vary together in the months observed, with no direction of effect established.
Ridership rises whenever a new shelter is opened, so each shelter adds a fixed number of riders.
options.misconception: Reads a correlation as a proven cause and effect.

options.text: The correlation proves that ridership cannot grow in this city unless shelters are built first.
options.misconception: Treats one correlated factor as the only route to the outcome.

options.text: Because the association is strong, next year's ridership can be predicted exactly from shelter counts.
options.misconception: Confuses a moderate association with exact prediction.

questions.explanation: The correlation shows only that the two quantities move together over the observed period. Shelter additions and rider growth may both follow from population growth, so the causal reading is unsupported.
questions.hint: Ask what else could make both numbers rise at once.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS

options.misconception: Attributes the whole pattern to a single convenient explanation.

options.text: Income, density, and car ownership differ across the distance bands, so proximity is not yet shown to reduce driving.
The distance bands were compared using self-reported driving, so the gap is a reporting artefact.
options.misconception: Dismisses a real association as pure measurement error.

options.text: Because the gap is clear, moving a station closer to homes would reduce car use by the same margin.
options.misconception: Generalises an observational gap into a forecast effect.

questions.explanation: Income, density, and car ownership differ across the distance bands, and any of them could produce the observed gap. Until those variables are matched or held constant, the association cannot be attributed to station proximity.
questions.hint: List what else differs between the distance bands.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Set out what evidence would justify a causal reading of an observed effect
questions.stem: A consultant presents a slide claiming that the agency's real-time arrival displays increased on-time performance by 12 points. Explain what evidence would be needed before the board treats that as a causal effect.

answer.exemplar: The board would need a comparison design in which some routes received the displays while comparable routes did not, so that performance could be compared between groups across the same period. Random assignment would be strongest. At minimum the consultant should report that displays are associated with better performance while checking whether weather, timetable redesign, or extra vehicles could explain the same gain.

questions.explanation: The slide has no comparison group, so seasonal trends and other simultaneous changes fold into the effect. Only a design that holds other factors constant can support a causal reading.
questions.hint: Ask where the counterfactual comes from.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute a raw change while noting that the compared groups were not equivalent
questions.stem: A route restructure is compared before and after, but the two periods drew different passengers because a school moved near the corridor. If daily ridership rose from 60 to 180, what is the raw percentage increase?
questions.explanation: The raw increase is (180 - 60) / 60, which equals 2, so ridership rose by 200 percent. Because the two periods involve different passenger populations, this raw figure cannot isolate the restructure's effect.
questions.hint: Compare the change against the earlier baseline.

options.misconception: Mistakes internal communication for an ethics safeguard.

options.text: Whether the timetable change will deliver the forecast savings in the agency budget.
options.misconception: Confuses ethics approval with a financial business case.

options.text: Whether the trial will produce results significant enough to justify a wider rollout.
options.misconception: Treats ethics clearance as a test of statistical significance.

options.text: Whether participants can consent freely, the risks are proportionate, and vulnerable riders are protected.

questions.explanation: Ethics review weighs recruitment pressure and group vulnerability against study risks and whether consent is genuinely voluntary. It judges protection and proportionality, not budget savings.

options.misconception: Misses that the deception itself blocks honest ratings.

options.text: Stop collecting data as soon as the first wave looks significant, then report that analysis alone.
options.misconception: Treats a favourable first result as a reason to stop.

options.text: Run whichever analysis best matches the second wave, since the registration was only a draft intention.
options.misconception: Treats the registered plan as freely revisable.

options.text: Pre-specify the analysis and stopping rule, then report the contradicting wave as a documented deviation.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a third variable can produce a spurious association
questions.stem: A planner reports that routes with more shelters have fewer complaints about missed connections. Explain how a third variable could produce this pattern without shelters doing any work.

answer.exemplar: Routes with more shelters are probably newer, better monitored corridors with more reliable schedules, so fewer complaints could reflect timetable quality or agency responsiveness rather than shelter provision. The planner should check whether complaint volumes track schedule reliability across routes, and note that complaint rates also vary with how actively riders report problems.

questions.explanation: A lurking variable is an unmeasured feature that pushes both the predictor and the outcome the same way. Without measuring it, the shelter effect and that third variable cannot be told apart in these data.
questions.hint: Ask what else these routes share.

questions.stem: In a staggered timetable trial, 30 of 60 improved routes receiving the new schedule met the punctuality target, and 18 of 60 comparison routes met it. What is the raw difference in percentage points between the two groups?
questions.explanation: Thirty of sixty is 50 percent and 18 of sixty is 30 percent, so the raw gap is 20 percentage points. Because assignment was not random, the gap estimates association rather than a proven causal effect.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the aims of debriefing and the harm of omitting it
questions.stem: Participants in a study about station signage were told they were testing a new colour scheme when they were actually shown the standard signs. Explain what the debriefing must achieve and why it cannot be skipped.

answer.exemplar: The debriefing must tell participants the true purpose of the study, correct the mistaken belief that the colour scheme was being tested, address any discomfort the false information caused, and restore their ability to withdraw their data or ask questions. Because the deception was needed for the study to work, the harm it created is removed only at debriefing, so skipping it leaves participants misinformed.

questions.explanation: Deception works by installing a false belief, so it is only undone when participants learn the truth and can revise their data. Skipping the debriefing leaves people misinformed and unable to object.
questions.hint: Ask what belief the deception installed.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose why a consent process failed to be genuinely voluntary
questions.stem: A study asks passengers to hand over their travel diary for a month and offers a chance to win a travel credit. Some participants later say they felt unable to refuse. Explain what went wrong with the consent process.

answer.exemplar: Consent is not only a signed form; it has to be free, informed, and understood. Offering a prize in a setting where people feel obliged or dependent on staff can make agreement feel compulsory, especially if refusal is awkward or undocumented. The agency should remove the pressure, explain that declining costs nothing, record refusals discreetly, and check at the end whether participants felt able to refuse.

questions.explanation: Consent fails when participants cannot realistically decline, whatever the paperwork says. An incentive combined with a sense of obligation undermines voluntariness and needs a genuine, easy way to refuse.
questions.hint: Ask what a participant's real options were.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a flawed comparison group biases an estimated effect
questions.stem: A comparison of the upgraded corridor with a neighbouring corridor shows 9 percent higher satisfaction on the upgraded route. Explain why this comparison may understate or overstate the upgrade's effect.

answer.exemplar: The two corridors differ in more than the upgrade: the comparison corridor serves a lower-income catchment, has older rolling stock, and runs a thinner evening service. If those differences favour the upgraded route, the 9 percent gap overstates the upgrade's effect; if they work against it, the gap understates it. The agency should compare pre-upgrade satisfaction on both corridors and match on those characteristics before reading the post-upgrade difference as the effect.

questions.explanation: A comparison group that differs on other characteristics leaves their contribution inside the observed gap, pushing the estimate up or down. Pre-upgrade baselines and matching are needed to isolate the upgrade.
questions.hint: Ask what the corridors looked like before the upgrade.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain a shared-cause account of an observed intervention effect
questions.stem: Fares were cut on three routes and ridership rose 15 percent on each of them. Explain how a third variable could explain the rise without the fare cut causing it.

answer.exemplar: All three routes ran through the same district, and that district opened a new office campus and a shopping centre in the same period. Employment and retail activity therefore rose on those routes regardless of price, so the fare cut and the ridership gain share a common cause. The agency would need to compare the same routes before the change and check similar routes elsewhere that had no fare cut.

questions.explanation: A shared cause moving both predictor and outcome makes them change together without a causal link. Separating the fare effect requires comparison with similar routes that kept their fares.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain what preregistration adds to a study with many outcomes
questions.stem: A team published a study of route performance with forty different outcome measures and no stated analysis plan. Explain what preregistration would have changed about this study.

answer.exemplar: A preregistration would have named one primary outcome, the model, the exclusions, and the stopping rule before the data were seen, so readers could tell planned findings from results discovered afterwards. With forty measures and no plan, the risk that a striking pattern was selected after the fact is high, and the uncertainty around any single reported estimate cannot be judged. The analysis would still run, but its status as confirmatory would be gone.

questions.explanation: Preregistration separates planned tests from results found by searching, and makes the uncertainty around any estimate judgeable. Without it, many outcomes make a striking result far less surprising.
questions.hint: Ask how many chances the search had to find a pattern.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why blanket permission for future data use is not informed consent
questions.stem: The consent form asks participants to agree that their travel records may be used for future studies. Explain what would make that consent valid rather than a blanket permission.

answer.exemplar: Consent to future use is valid when participants are told in advance what kinds of studies would use their records, who would run them, whether their identity will be visible, and how long the data will be kept. Blanket wording that transfers ownership to the agency removes real choices at the moment of consent. A better approach describes the categories of future use, mentions the option to decline future use while taking part now, and repeats the choice in each later study.

questions.explanation: Consent is about informed choice, so a catch-all permission leaves participants no real decision and is not properly informed. Naming intended uses and their limits keeps the agreement meaningful.
questions.hint: Ask what choice the participant actually gets to make.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Set out what a defensible causal claim would require from the agency
questions.stem: A survey shows that routes with more frequent service have higher satisfaction, and a manager wants to build the causal case before the next budget round. Explain what a defensible causal claim would require.

answer.exemplar: A defensible claim needs a design that could have produced the result other ways. The strongest option is random assignment of the timetable change across comparable routes, with satisfaction measured before and after on both sets. Without randomisation the agency could use matched routes plus an interrupted time series and would have to state clearly that residual confounding remains. The budget paper should present the association, name the third variables it cannot exclude, and describe the design it intends to use next.

questions.explanation: A causal claim needs evidence that the association would not appear without the service change, requiring a comparison that rules out rival explanations. Observational data support a bounded claim only.
questions.hint: Ask what design would make the rival explanations unlikely.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a sound preregistration policy treats forced deviations
questions.stem: A team argues that preregistration forbids any change to an analysis plan, even when a data error is discovered mid-study. Explain how a sound preregistration policy handles this case.

answer.exemplar: A sound policy separates deviations that are opportunistic from those that are forced by a genuine data problem. A documented correction for a known error is legitimate, but it must be recorded with its date, its reason, and its effect on the analysis, and reported alongside the registered plan. What is forbidden is changing the plan because a preferred result was unavailable, and a policy that allows none of this would simply push teams to misreport their data.

questions.explanation: Preregistration constrains choices made in response to results, not corrections forced by data errors. Policy should require transparent documentation of any change so readers can judge the analysis.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change was forced by the data or by the result.

options.misconception: Refuses the association that the data do support.

questions.explanation: The comparison supports a description of higher satisfaction on the express corridor. Because service, shelters, marketing, and survey timing changed together, no single element can be identified as the cause.
questions.hint: Count the changes that moved together.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Choose the comparison design that best supports an upgrade decision
questions.stem: Which pairing would give the board the most defensible comparison of the upgraded corridor with an untreated route?

options.text: An upgraded corridor and a different corridor measured after the upgrade, since after-only data is simplest.
options.misconception: Accepts a design with no baseline information at all.

options.text: An upgraded corridor and the largest route in the network, because the bigger sample proves more.
options.misconception: Mistakes a large sample for a comparable group.

options.text: An upgraded corridor and the route with the worst results, to make the upgrade look impressive.
options.misconception: Describes a deliberately unfair comparison as informative.

options.text: An upgraded corridor and a similar corridor with similar ridership, income mix, and service levels before the upgrade.

questions.explanation: Comparability before treatment is what makes a difference interpretable, so groups should match on ridership, income mix, and service levels. Sample size does not compensate for groups that differed beforehand.
questions.hint: Ask which route looked most like the upgraded one before.
